ca-0G0L.title: Google car: overcast Gen 2 high in the mountains
ca-0G0L.summary: The Top of the World Highway, west of Dawson City in Yukon, has overcast Gen 2 coverage high up in the mountains.

ca-0Ohz.title: Landscape: dense forest, mountains, overcast
ca-0Ohz.summary: The inland Gaspé Peninsula roads have densely forested mountains and frequent overcast coverage.

ca-0rfu.title: Landscape: forested highland with mixed trees
ca-0rfu.summary: The Cape Breton Highlands in northeast Nova Scotia are unusually high for the east and heavily forested with broadleaf and pine trees.

ca-2bbX.title: Houses: very tall water tower with town name
ca-2bbX.summary: Town water towers are very tall and sometimes have the town's name on them. The same in the US.

ca-3TFG.title: Road lines: white dashes between yellow lines
ca-3TFG.summary: In Saskatchewan you can sometimes find white dashes between the yellow centre lines. They also appear rarely in British Columbia and Yukon, where the landscape is very different.

ca-3vxs.title: Bollard: flat yellow
ca-3vxs.summary: Flat yellow bollards on the main highway in New Brunswick.

ca-4Kbc.title: Plate: short plate, no blue strip
ca-4Kbc.summary: Short licence plates like the US. Europe uses long plates with a blue strip. Each province has its own design.

ca-5pb9.title: Landscape: coast in view, red soil, white houses
ca-5pb9.summary: Red Bay, on the south coast of Labrador, always shows the coast, with slightly red soil and mostly white houses.

ca-6BuB.title: Landscape: barren hills and river valleys
ca-6BuB.summary: Southern Saskatchewan has many river valleys and so can be barren and hilly, unlike the very flat rest of the Great Plains. Some of this reaches southern Alberta and Manitoba.

ca-6tmz.title: Mailbox: on a post with a small flag
ca-6tmz.summary: A mailbox on top of a post with a small flag on the side points to North America.

ca-7Oi3.title: Bollard: rectangular roadside markers
ca-7Oi3.summary: Rectangular markers beside the road in Québec, in varying colours. Rarely seen on divided urban highways in New Brunswick.

ca-7Q8P.title: Landscape: treeless canyon rock formations
ca-7Q8P.summary: Near Drumheller, Alberta: canyon-like treeless rock formations.

ca-7vrj.title: Google car: group of motorcyclists ahead
ca-7vrj.summary: A group of motorcyclists rides in front of the Google car on Highway 1 near Beaver Creek in Yukon.

ca-8sEO.title: Bollard: thin curved black-and-white
ca-8sEO.summary: A thin, slightly curved black-and-white bollard, most common on Vancouver Island but across British Columbia. It can look like Alberta's, but is thinner with wider-spaced black bands.

ca-8xOs.title: Landscape: boreal hills, thin short conifers
ca-8xOs.summary: A northern boreal landscape, mostly hilly with sometimes big mountains far off. Conifers line the roads and get thinner and shorter further north. Older Gen 2 coverage is common.

ca-9HIG.title: Google car: thin antenna on front right
ca-9HIG.summary: The remote town of Churchill in northern Manitoba has a trekker with a thin antenna on the front right, and unique street signs. The surrounding area also has this coverage.

ca-ATJW.title: Bin: wooden plank bin, often octagonal
ca-ATJW.summary: Wooden plank bins on driveways are most common in Newfoundland, usually octagonal. Sometimes seen in other provinces such as New Brunswick.

ca-B83g.title: Landscape: flat plains, few trees
ca-B83g.summary: The Great Plains are mostly flat with some rolling hills, lots of farming, hardly any trees and very few people. It gets drier to the south-southwest, driest near Montana.

differs.how: Looks similar to the northern US plains

ca-BSBp.title: Bollard: cylinder with thick black bands
ca-BSBp.summary: In the Northwest Territories, a black-and-white cylinder with two thick black bands. Alberta's looks similar but has thinner black bands.

ca-C7EA.title: Sign: stop sign says STOP and ARRÊT
ca-C7EA.summary: Stop signs with both STOP and ARRÊT are most common in New Brunswick, and rare in other provinces.

ca-D1Vh.title: Marker: diamond sign beside a fire hydrant
ca-D1Vh.summary: Newfoundland fire hydrants often have a diamond-shaped marker next to them.

ca-DPnH.title: Direction sign: hanging from unique signposts
ca-DPnH.summary: British Columbia signs are sometimes hung down from this unique style of signpost.

ca-DXYT.title: Guardrail: concrete barriers instead
ca-DXYT.summary: British Columbia mostly uses concrete barriers instead of guardrails.

ca-DqvA.title: Sign: speed sign says MAXIMUM
ca-DqvA.summary: Speed signs say MAXIMUM on one line, and kilometre numbers look higher than US ones. US signs say SPEED LIMIT on two lines and more often end in 5.

differs.how: US signs say SPEED LIMIT on two lines

ca-FCIr.title: Road: remote, thin pines, low sun, sunny Gen 4
ca-FCIr.summary: The Trans-Labrador Highway (roads 500 and 510) has sunny Gen 4 coverage, thin pines, a remote cold feel and often a low sun. Past Happy Valley-Goose Bay you often see snow on the ground.

ca-FxqV.title: Pole: insulator raised on top of the pole
ca-FxqV.summary: An insulator raised slightly on top of the pole, especially on simple single-insulator poles, suggests the US or Canada and is not typical in Europe.

ca-GAxI.title: Bollard: cylinder with two black bands
ca-GAxI.summary: A cylindrical bollard with two black bands wrapping all the way round, often at intersections. Appears in Alberta very often. Some have a yellow middle band, and rarely blue (around Calgary) or green (around Edmonton).

ca-GjWG.title: Bollard: black and grey, orange stripe
ca-GjWG.summary: Black and grey painted bollards, usually with an orange stripe below the grey. Wooden rectangular ones are further north in Manitoba. Bollards with just a black top also appear in Saskatchewan.

ca-IqjC.title: Landscape: distinct mountains, red-tinted soil
ca-IqjC.summary: Qikiqtarjuaq has distinct mountains and red-tinted soil.

ca-Izqw.title: Sign: held up by wooden boxes
ca-Izqw.summary: Signs in Newfoundland and Labrador are propped up in wooden boxes.

ca-J4W5.title: Sign: green backs of road signs
ca-J4W5.summary: In British Columbia, road signs can have green backs. Also fairly common on Prince Edward Island.

ca-JHUC.title: Lamp: short curved arm on utility pole
ca-JHUC.summary: Nova Scotia's utility-pole lamp arms are usually curved and much shorter than in the rest of Canada. Short arms occasionally appear elsewhere.

ca-JWTI.title: Direction sign: white triangles on the post
ca-JWTI.summary: Saskatchewan signposts can carry white triangles, the number varies.

ca-KYOQ.title: Direction sign: thin metal post, holes or U shape
ca-KYOQ.summary: Thin metal signposts are common, with several small holes or a U-shaped profile.

ca-KwMJ.title: Road lines: double yellow common in the east
ca-KwMJ.summary: In Eastern Canada double yellow lines are most common in Nova Scotia, then Québec and Prince Edward Island. Ontario prefers single yellow but sometimes uses double.

ca-L5qh.title: Plants: balsam fir, Christmas-tree look
ca-L5qh.summary: Balsam fir is very common in Newfoundland and looks like a Christmas tree. It also grows elsewhere in eastern Canada and the US.

ca-L8XW.title: Pole: insulators alternate pole to pole
ca-L8XW.summary: In Saskatchewan, one pole has one insulator on the left and two on the right, and the next has the reverse. Rarely seen in Manitoba.

ca-LqkP.title: Language: colour, centre, kilometres
ca-LqkP.summary: English-speaking areas use British spelling (colour, centre) and metric units such as km/h. The US uses American spelling and usually miles.

differs.how: US uses American spelling and miles

ca-MiOa.title: Road lines: single yellow centre line
ca-MiOa.summary: Mostly a single yellow centre line, though double yellow is fairly common too. Double yellow is more common in the US, so this is not fully reliable.

differs.how: US uses double yellow more often

ca-MwL1.title: Pole: wooden, big metal cylinder transformer
ca-MwL1.summary: North America mostly uses wooden poles, with large metal cylinder transformers that never appear in Europe. Concrete poles suggest Europe.

ca-Npc7.title: Soil: red tint, potato farms
ca-Npc7.summary: Prince Edward Island soil has a distinct red tint and potato farming is common. Red soil also occasionally appears in parts of New Brunswick and Nova Scotia.

ca-NqxH.title: Flags: provincial flags, Fleurdelisé
ca-NqxH.summary: Provincial flags appear fairly often. Québec's Fleurdelisé is especially common.

ca-OoKB.title: Guardrail: small posts with 3 or 4 wires
ca-OoKB.summary: A guardrail of small poles joined by three or four metal wires, rarely on major highways in Alberta.

ca-Qpy3.title: Lamp: rectangular lamp heads
ca-Qpy3.summary: New Brunswick and Nova Scotia often have rectangular lamp heads.

ca-Qvdu.title: Sign: bilingual street signs
ca-Qvdu.summary: New Brunswick street signs are bilingual. Unlike stop signs, bilingual street signs also appear in other French-minority areas.

ca-RMBK.title: Google car: Gen 3 with two mirror peaks
ca-RMBK.summary: Gen 3 is much more common than in the US. The blurred side mirrors usually show as two peaks here, while the US mostly shows a single peak.

differs.how: US Gen 3 mirrors usually show a single peak

ca-Rqw0.title: Landscape: dry hills, brown grass, pines
ca-Rqw0.summary: In the southern interior of British Columbia around Kamloops and Kelowna: hilly and a bit drier, with sprawling brown grassland and pine forests on the slopes.

ca-TOm0.title: Coverage: snowmobile with driver in brown coat
ca-TOm0.summary: Sanikiluaq, a remote town in Hudson Bay, was covered by a snowmobile whose driver wears a dark brown coat. On the ice outside town the driver is not visible.

ca-ThNh.title: Street sign: signals and signs on hanging bars
ca-ThNh.summary: At big intersections, long metal bars hold traffic lights over the street and often street or highway signs too. The same in the US.

ca-U1I1.title: Landscape: green rocky hills, distant trees
ca-U1I1.summary: Kangiqsualujjuaq in northern Québec is surrounded by green rocky hills with trees in the distance.

ca-UJ8K.title: Google car: unique car, dark soil
ca-UJ8K.summary: A unique car and dark soil in Tulita, Northwest Territories. The car is often fully blurred with only the antenna or the hood showing.

ca-UjZq.title: Pole: two hanging insulators
ca-UjZq.summary: Poles with two hanging insulators are common in Manitoba.

ca-W3WH.title: Landscape: flat green farmland, densely populated
ca-W3WH.summary: The Québec City to Windsor corridor is the most densely populated part. It is mostly flat and green with farmland and occasional forest. It can look like the US Great Lakes region.

differs.how: Looks similar to the US Great Lakes region

ca-W97X.title: Pole: transformer at 45 degrees
ca-W97X.summary: On Prince Edward Island and Nova Scotia, transformers sit at a 45 degree angle to the road. On PEI, red numbers are usually written on the side.

ca-X21k.title: Bollard: tall white pole, red or green reflector
ca-X21k.summary: Québec bollards are always attached to guardrails: long, thin white poles with a red or green reflector at the top.

ca-Xhjx.title: Direction sign: green and white striped sticker
ca-Xhjx.summary: Manitoba signposts sometimes carry a green and white striped sticker.

ca-Xmvk.title: Plate: each province has its own
ca-Xmvk.summary: Every province has its own plates, some recognisable even when blurred. Several provinces do not require front plates. New Brunswick dropped front plates in 2019, and Newfoundland and Labrador commercial vehicles still need them.

ca-ZXpA.title: Landscape: N-S grid, farms among birch forest
ca-ZXpA.summary: Around Rouyn-Noranda in northwest Québec: a north-south road grid, slightly hilly with farm fields between forests of short trees and thin birches.

ca-a1P6.title: Kilometre marker: white square at the bottom
ca-a1P6.summary: Each province has slightly different kilometre markers. Ontario's have a white square at the bottom, unique to it.

ca-a6DY.title: Landscape: barren with snow patches
ca-a6DY.summary: Resolute, in the far north, has a barren landscape with patches of snow.

ca-avt6.title: Coverage: Gen 2 trekker
ca-avt6.summary: Cambridge Bay is the only Nunavut settlement with Gen 2 trekker coverage.

ca-b7hs.title: Mailbox: communal boxes, red Canada Post logo
ca-b7hs.summary: Communal mailboxes appear sometimes, though personal ones are still common. Canada Post has a red logo. Communal boxes are very rare in the US, whose postal logo is blue.

differs.how: US has few communal boxes and a blue logo

ca-bfXS.title: Sign: stop sign says ARRÊT
ca-bfXS.summary: Stop signs with only the word ARRÊT are unique to Québec.

ca-by9f.title: Pole: insulators pointing toward the road
ca-by9f.summary: Insulators facing toward or away from the road are mostly in Québec, Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island. Elsewhere they face along the road. Most reliable away from junctions and driveways.

ca-c5Ap.title: Plants: bright yellow canola fields
ca-c5Ap.summary: Canola, like fields of bright yellow flowers, grows in the central southern prairies and almost nowhere else in Canada. Also very common in North Dakota.

ca-dCuR.title: Direction sign: yellow hydrant marker on top
ca-dCuR.summary: Yellow fire hydrant markers sit on top of signposts in Québec. In Québec City they usually have a blue rectangle and in Trois-Rivières they are small. Colours can vary. Edmundston in New Brunswick has them too.

ca-eMcz.title: Flag: tricolour with yellow star in blue
ca-eMcz.summary: Acadia is a French-speaking region in the Maritimes, mainly north and east New Brunswick plus some communities in Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island. Its flag is a tricolour with a yellow star in the blue band, flown or painted on poles.

ca-f2ba.title: Route marker: Township and Range road numbers
ca-f2ba.summary: Alberta's rural roads are numbered in a grid. Township roads (Twp Rd) run east-west and rise going north; range roads (Rge Rd) run north-south and rise going west, resetting a few times. Multiply the grid numbers by 10 to get road numbers. Saskatchewan has some too.

ca-gj69.title: Guardrail: wooden posts with pyramid tops
ca-gj69.summary: In Newfoundland and Labrador, most wooden guardrail posts have a pyramid-shaped top. Occasionally also on free-standing posts and signposts.

ca-gyfH.title: Coverage: snowmobile seen through the blur
ca-gyfH.summary: Inukjuak in northern Québec has a snowmobile visible through the blur. In Sanikiluaq, the other snowmobile town, the driver is always visible.

ca-hHgh.title: Language: French in the east, bilingual signs
ca-hHgh.summary: French is the majority language in Québec and parts of New Brunswick. French is official nationally, so bilingual signs appear elsewhere, and French is spoken in some communities in Nova Scotia, Ontario and Manitoba.

ca-hVpY.title: Road: unpaved, dark brown soil, tundra
ca-hVpY.summary: The Dempster Highway (roads 5 and 8) links Yukon to Inuvik in the Northwest Territories. It is unpaved with Gen 2 coverage, dark brown soil and tundra with short trees, hilly then flat between Fort McPherson and Inuvik, and cloudier near Inuvik.

ca-iAnh.title: Route marker: each province has its own shield
ca-iAnh.summary: Each province has its own highway shield design. The green Trans-Canada Highway shield appears in all 10 provinces.

ca-iRPW.title: Sign: T-junction sign without chequerboard
ca-iRPW.summary: Québec's T-intersection signs do not have the chequerboard pattern.

ca-ivWy.title: Street sign: turquoise bilingual
ca-ivWy.summary: Iqaluit, the capital of Nunavut, is more built up than other settlements, with bilingual turquoise street signs, bilingual speed limit signs, and unique road markers on the outskirts.

ca-jkB6.title: Google car: Gen 2, big round blur, sky halo
ca-jkB6.summary: A fair amount of Gen 2 coverage, especially rural and remote: big round car blur and a halo-like colour distortion in the sky. Gen 2 is very rare in the US, so near the border it points here.

differs.how: Gen 2 is very rare in the US

ca-jz1c.title: Houses: colourful wooden houses, trees, big hill
ca-jz1c.summary: Nain, a small town on the northeast coast of Labrador, has colourful wooden houses and trees. A big hill is usually visible to the north and rocky cliffs across the bay to the south. Kids sometimes walk beside the trekker.

ca-kj4w.title: Coverage: overcast autumn Gen 3, snow, smudge
ca-kj4w.summary: Roads QC-167 and QC-113 have overcast autumn Gen 3 coverage, often with snow on the ground, and a smudge on the image.

ca-kxon.title: Road lines: rumble strips in the middle
ca-kxon.summary: Rumble strips in the middle of the road, usually over the lines, are most common in Alberta and British Columbia.

ca-l2KH.title: Pole: small white sticker
ca-l2KH.summary: Poles on Prince Edward Island usually have a small white sticker.

ca-lFnl.title: Landscape: exposed rocks of the Shield
ca-lFnl.summary: The Canadian Shield covers the eastern part of the country, so bare rock is common in the highlighted area.

ca-lSxm.title: Google car: low camera, big round blur, mirror
ca-lSxm.summary: A low-mounted Gen 4 camera with a big round blur and a small bump at the front, sometimes see-through. When badly blurred, a mirror sticks out on the right. The US has it too.

ca-lWyG.title: Plants: aspen trees, yellow in fall
ca-lWyG.summary: Aspens are common in forested parts of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta, with white birch-like trunks. They turn bright yellow in fall coverage.

ca-lm-179.title: Sign: double warning sign post
ca-lm-179.summary: Warning signs mounted on a double signpost are unique to Québec in Canada.

ca-mVCj.title: Route marker: rural roads with N, E or W suffix
ca-mVCj.summary: Manitoba's rural roads are on a grid, named by number and direction. Roads ending in N run east-west and rise one per mile north of the US border; E or W roads run north-south and give distance from the meridian just west of Winnipeg.

ca-nQn9.title: Landscape: big mountains
ca-nQn9.summary: The west is very mountainous. The highest mountains are in British Columbia, western Alberta and parts of Yukon. Elsewhere large mountains are rare or absent.

ca-nuXI.title: Landscape: unique mountains and ice floes
ca-nuXI.summary: Grise Fiord, the northernmost covered town in Canada, has unique mountains and ice floes along the coast.

ca-oiV6.title: Road: SSW to NNE, washed-out lines, fir forest
ca-oiV6.summary: Route 430 in Newfoundland runs south-southwest to north-northeast with slightly faded lines in a remote area. You often see the coast to the west and low balsam fir forest to the east, sometimes a wall of mountains.

ca-pK0p.title: Pole: transformer faces the road
ca-pK0p.summary: Transformers face the road in British Columbia and New Brunswick. In other provinces they sit parallel with the wires.

ca-s9c4.title: Bollard: diamond-shaped roadside markers
ca-s9c4.summary: Diamond-shaped markers beside the road in Ontario, in varying colours.

ca-sOVD.title: Coverage: glacier in barren rocky land
ca-sOVD.summary: The world's northernmost Street View, a trekker on Ellesmere Island, shows a glacier in a rocky landscape with no plants. It is sometimes added to competitive maps to widen the scoring range, though you cannot pinpoint it.

ca-stpJ.title: Traffic cones: orange and black stripes
ca-stpJ.summary: Ontario uses orange-and-black striped cones. Québec has orange-and-white striped ones.

ca-tfjm.title: Chevron: red and white
ca-tfjm.summary: Québec is the only province with red and white chevrons. The rest of Canada uses yellow and black.

ca-uDWd.title: Sign: blank yield and rail signs
ca-uDWd.summary: Canadian signs have fewer words. Yield and railroad signs are typically blank, while US ones spell out YIELD or RAILROAD CROSSING.

differs.how: US signs spell out YIELD and RAILROAD CROSSING

ca-vONr.title: Pole: black and yellow label with a Q
ca-vONr.summary: Québec poles may have a vertical black and yellow label with a small Q in the black part.

ca-wJ1d.title: Phone numbers: 3-digit area code
ca-wJ1d.summary: Numbers start with a 3-digit area code, the same for landlines and mobiles, written XXX XXX XXXX. 7-digit numbers with the area code left out are fairly common.

ca-wU0C.title: Pole: insulator rods angled upward
ca-wU0C.summary: Some Québec poles have tops with insulator rods angled slightly upward.

ca-wU9H.title: Speed sign: black bottom panel or French text
ca-wU9H.summary: Some provinces have special speed signs: Ontario's may have a black panel with km/h or BEGINS in white; British Columbia's show km/h without the black panel; Québec's sometimes use French.

ca-xFTb.title: Guardrail: wooden posts with three wires
ca-xFTb.summary: Ontario often has round wooden posts joined by exactly three metal wires. Some posts have a reflective white band.

ca-xlem.title: Landscape: sharp mountain peaks on both sides
ca-xlem.summary: Highway 93 through Banff and Jasper parks has gradual and steep mountains with a sharp peak either side of the road, and tall, thin trees.

ca-yepj.title: Sign: T-junction with yellow rectangle border
ca-yepj.summary: Newfoundland T-intersection signs have a rectangular yellow border around the diamond.

ca-z3w1.title: Pole: two side insulators and one on top
ca-z3w1.summary: Two insulators to the side, held by a distinct attachment, and one on top, most common in Ontario. Several can be stacked. Occasionally seen in British Columbia, Nova Scotia and rarely elsewhere.

ca-zycw.title: Sign: diamond-shaped T-junction sign
ca-zycw.summary: T-intersection warning signs are diamond-shaped, found only in this country. The US uses rectangular ones.
